blocks.text: 1. ICE Plots

blocks.alt: Each individual row traces its own line as one feature varies

blocks.text: A Partial Dependence Plot, the immediately preceding topic, averages one feature's effect across the entire dataset into a single, summarized line. Individual Conditional Expectation plots, commonly abbreviated ICE, show that exact same underlying relationship separately, for every single individual instance in the dataset, rather than collapsing everything down into one averaged line.

The result is one line per data point, rather than one averaged line for the whole dataset, directly revealing whether the Partial Dependence Plot's averaged line is actually a fair, representative summary, or whether it is quietly hiding meaningfully different individual behaviors underneath a single, tidy-looking average.
2. Building an ICE Plot

blocks.alt: One specific row has its feature swept, tracing one individual curve

blocks.text: Building an Individual Conditional Expectation plot starts by picking one specific data instance and one feature to examine, then varying that feature across a range of test values, exactly the same mechanism already covered for Partial Dependence Plots in the previous topic. The model predicts on this one instance at each test value, holding every other feature fixed at its own real, original value for that instance specifically.

Plotting the resulting curve traces out how this one instance's prediction changes as the chosen feature varies, and repeating this entire process for many individual instances, overlaying every resulting curve on the same shared plot, produces the final Individual Conditional Expectation visualization, a genuinely richer picture than any single averaged line could offer alone.
3. The Direct Relationship to Partial Dependence Plots

blocks.alt: Averaging every individual ICE curve produces the partial dependence plot

blocks.text: This connects directly back to Partial Dependence Plots, the immediately preceding topic. A Partial Dependence Plot line is, mathematically, literally the average of every single Individual Conditional Expectation curve in the dataset, computed at each test value along the feature's range.

An Individual Conditional Expectation plot shows the full underlying spread that average is actually computed from, information the Partial Dependence Plot alone genuinely cannot reveal on its own. The Partial Dependence Plot alone cannot distinguish between a spread that is narrow and consistent across every instance, versus one that is wide and genuinely divergent, exactly the gap Individual Conditional Expectation plots are built to fill.

blocks.text: 4. What the Spread Reveals

blocks.alt: Curves that spread apart reveal that rows behave differently from each other

blocks.text: When every individual curve in an Individual Conditional Expectation plot points in roughly the same direction, rising together or falling together in a broadly consistent pattern, the corresponding Partial Dependence Plot's average is a fair, genuinely representative summary of how the whole dataset actually behaves.

But when the curves point in genuinely different directions, some rising while others fall, or diverging sharply in shape, an interaction effect is hiding underneath that average, one the Partial Dependence Plot alone would miss entirely, since averaging opposite-direction curves together can produce a deceptively flat or misleadingly moderate-looking average line.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A flat-looking Partial Dependence Plot line does not necessarily mean a feature has no effect. It can instead mean the feature has a strong effect that points in opposite directions for different instances, canceling out in the average, exactly the kind of hidden pattern an ICE plot exposes.

blocks.text: 5. Revealing Interaction Effects Without Guessing

blocks.alt: ICE plots reveal interaction effects that a single average curve would hide

blocks.text: This connects back to the two-feature Partial Dependence Plot's interaction-effect view, covered in the previous topic. That two-feature approach requires deliberately picking a second feature in advance to check for an interaction with, a real limitation when the analyst does not yet know which second feature might be involved.

Individual Conditional Expectation plots reveal interaction effects too, but without needing to pick that second feature ahead of time at all. Diverging individual curves are themselves direct, immediate evidence that some other feature in the dataset is genuinely changing the examined feature's effect, pointing the analyst toward further investigation without requiring an upfront guess.
6. Centered ICE Plots

blocks.alt: Every curve gets anchored at the same starting point, becoming a centered ICE plot

blocks.text: A Centered Individual Conditional Expectation plot anchors every single curve to zero at one common starting point, typically the feature's minimum test value, rather than leaving each curve at its own instance's natural, differing baseline prediction level.

This removes each instance's differing starting height from the picture entirely, making it considerably easier to compare the shape of each curve's change across the feature's range, rather than being distracted by which instance simply started with a higher or lower baseline prediction to begin with. Centering is particularly useful when a dataset's instances have widely varying baseline predictions that would otherwise dominate the visual comparison.
7. A Genuine Weakness: Overplotting

blocks.alt: Too many individual curves lead to overplotting

blocks.text: A genuine, practical weakness of Individual Conditional Expectation plots is that plotting one curve per instance for a large dataset produces overwhelming visual clutter. Hundreds or thousands of overlapping lines drawn on the same plot become genuinely unreadable, defeating the entire purpose of visualizing individual behavior in the first place.

The common, practical fix is to plot only a representative random sample of instances, perhaps 50 to 100 curves, rather than every single one in the dataset, preserving enough individual detail to spot genuine divergence while keeping the plot visually readable.
8. The Same Unrealistic-Combination Weakness

This connects directly back to the exact unrealistic-combination weakness already covered for Partial Dependence Plots in the previous topic. Individual Conditional Expectation plots inherit that identical weakness, since they use the same underlying mechanism of varying one feature while holding every other feature fixed.

Varying one feature for a single instance while holding its other features fixed at their real, original values can still create feature combinations that would rarely or never genuinely occur in real, actual data, exactly the same correlated-feature caveat that applies to Partial Dependence Plots, and originally to Permutation Importance before that.
9. When ICE Plots Are the Right Choice

Individual Conditional Expectation plots are the right choice specifically for checking whether a Partial Dependence Plot's average is actually representative of the whole dataset, the single most direct, purpose-built use case this technique was designed for.

They are also the right choice when an analyst suspects an interaction effect exists but does not yet know which second feature is involved, since diverging curves point directly at heterogeneity worth investigating further without requiring an upfront guess. And they suit explaining model behavior for a small number of specific, named instances directly, showing exactly how each one individually would respond to a changing feature value.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: In practice, Individual Conditional Expectation and Partial Dependence Plots are almost always shown together on the same axes, the averaged Partial Dependence Plot line overlaid directly on top of its underlying ICE curves, combining both the summary and the full spread in one single view.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below computes Individual Conditional Expectation curves for a handful of instances alongside the averaged Partial Dependence Plot line, directly comparing the spread to the average.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.uniform(500, 5000, size=(300, 2))
y = 50000 + 150 * X[:, 0] - 800 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(scale=20000, size=300)

model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)

result = partial_dependence(model, X, features=[0], kind="both", grid_resolution=10)
test_values = result['grid_values'][0]
ice_curves = result['individual'][0]      # one row per instance
average_curve = result['average'][0]      # the Partial Dependence Plot line

curve_spread = ice_curves[:, -1].std()
print(f"Spread of individual predictions at the highest test value: {curve_spread:,.0f}")
print(f"Averaged Partial Dependence Plot prediction at the same point: {average_curve[-1]:,.0f}")

if curve_spread < average_curve[-1] * 0.1:
    print("Narrow spread: the averaged line is a fair, representative summary")
else:
    print("Wide spread: individual instances diverge, worth investigating further")

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: The kind="both" argument to scikit-learn's partial_dependence function returns both the individual ICE curves and the averaged Partial Dependence Plot line together, exactly the combined view most practical workflows rely on.

blocks.text: 11. Explainable AI: Key Takeaways

items: ICE plots show one curve per individual instance, rather than one averaged curve for the whole dataset.
A Partial Dependence Plot line is literally the average of every ICE curve at each test value.
Consistent curve directions mean the average is representative; diverging curves reveal a hidden interaction effect.
ICE reveals interaction effects without needing to pick a second feature in advance, unlike two-feature Partial Dependence Plots.
Centered ICE plots anchor every curve to zero, making shape comparison easier than comparing absolute starting height.
Overplotting is a genuine weakness for large datasets; the fix is plotting a representative random sample of instances.
ICE inherits the same unrealistic-combination weakness already covered for Partial Dependence Plots and Permutation Importance.
